content: The recommendations outlined in this report build upon previous guidelines aimed at preventing hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, which primarily focused on the screening and follow-up of blood, plasma, organ, tissue, and semen donors. These updated recommendations provide a more comprehensive framework for preventing HCV transmission, identifying and counseling individuals at risk, and ensuring appropriate medical evaluation and management for those infected with HCV. The guidelines were developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in collaboration with experts who convened in Atlanta in July 1998. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is the most prevalent chronic bloodborne infection in the United States. During the 1980s, an estimated 230,000 new infections occurred annually. Approximately 1.8% of Americans have been infected with HCV, with most cases being chronic. Many individuals remain unaware of their infection due to the absence of clinical symptoms. These individuals serve as a source of transmission to others and are at risk of developing chronic liver disease or other HCV-related complications over the course of decades following initial infection. Chronic liver disease is the 10th leading cause of death among adults in the United States, accounting for approximately 25,000 deaths annually, or about 1% of all deaths. Studies suggest that 40% of chronic liver disease cases are HCV-related, resulting in an estimated 8,000–10,000 deaths each year. The annual medical and work-loss costs associated with HCV-related liver disease exceed $600 million, and HCV-associated end-stage liver disease is the leading indication for liver transplantation among adults. As most HCV-infected individuals are aged 30–49 years, the number of deaths attributable to HCV-related liver disease is expected to rise significantly over the next 10–20 years as this population ages and complications from chronic liver disease emerge. HCV is primarily transmitted through large or repeated direct percutaneous exposures to blood. In the United States, the relative importance of the two most common exposure routes—blood transfusion and injecting drug use—has shifted over time. Blood transfusion, which accounted for a significant proportion of HCV infections acquired more than a decade ago, now rarely contributes to new infections due to improved screening measures. Since 1994, the risk of transfusion-transmitted HCV infection has been so low that no cases of acute hepatitis C associated with transfusion have been detected in CDC surveillance systems, although the risk is not zero. In contrast, injecting drug use remains a major contributor to HCV transmission, accounting for 60% of new infections in the United States. Despite a decline in the incidence of acute hepatitis C since 1989, a high proportion of infections continue to be associated with injecting drug use. The decline in acute hepatitis C cases among injecting drug users is not fully understood but may reflect changes in behavior or other factors. Reducing the burden of HCV infection and its associated diseases in the United States requires the implementation of primary prevention strategies to reduce the risk of acquiring HCV and secondary prevention measures to mitigate the risk of liver and other chronic diseases in HCV-infected individuals. The recommendations in this report are based on a review of current data and expert opinions and provide broad guidelines for addressing these challenges. HCV infection occurs across all age groups, but the highest incidence of acute hepatitis C is observed among individuals aged 20–39 years, with a slight predominance in males. African Americans and whites have similar incidence rates of acute disease, while individuals of Hispanic ethnicity have higher rates. In the general population, the highest prevalence of HCV infection is found among individuals aged 30–49 years and among males. African Americans have a substantially higher prevalence of HCV infection compared to whites. The prevalence of HCV infection varies significantly among populations with different risk factors. High prevalence rates are observed among injecting drug users, individuals with hemophilia treated with clotting factor concentrates before 1987, and recipients of transfusions from HCV-positive donors. Long-term hemodialysis patients and healthcare workers are also at increased risk, although the prevalence among healthcare workers is similar to that of the general population. Occupational exposure, particularly through needlestick injuries, is a recognized risk factor for HCV infection. HCV transmission through sexual activity is inefficient but does occur. Case-control studies have identified an association between sexual exposure to an infected partner or multiple partners and acquiring HCV. However, the prevalence of HCV infection among long-term spouses of individuals with chronic HCV infection is low, raising questions about the role of sexual activity in HCV transmission. More data are needed to clarify the risk factors and mechanisms of sexual transmission. Household contact with an HCV-infected individual is another potential route of transmission, likely through direct or inapparent percutaneous exposure to infectious blood. However, transmission in this setting appears to be uncommon. Perinatal transmission occurs in approximately 5%–6% of infants born to HCV-positive, HIV-negative women, with higher rates observed among infants born to women coinfected with HCV and HIV. The presence of HCV RNA in the mother at the time of delivery is the primary factor associated with transmission. Breastfeeding has not been shown to transmit HCV. Diagnostic tests for HCV infection, including enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) and recombinant immunoblot assays (RIBAs), are used to detect anti-HCV antibodies. These tests do not distinguish between acute, chronic, or resolved infections. HCV RNA testing, performed using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), can detect the virus within 1–2 weeks of exposure and is particularly useful for confirming active infection. However, no FDA-approved RT-PCR assays are currently available for clinical use.
